Chapter overview

Study the Sangam Age through a clear sequence of dynasties, rulers, inscriptions, administration, warfare, agriculture, trade, foreign accounts and religion. The final revision section focuses on precise ruler–title, dynasty–port and inscription–association links.

SourcesDynastiesState & economyTrade & transition
Period, Extent and Historical Sources

The Sangam Age is conventionally dated between 300 BCE and 300 CE. Tamilakam was politically diverse, and its history is reconstructed by comparing literary, inscriptional, foreign, archaeological and numismatic evidence.

Period and Extent

The Sangam Age is conventionally placed between 300 BCE and 300 CE.

Ancient Tamilakam extended:

  • From Vengadam in the north
  • To Kumari in the south
  • Between the eastern and western seas

Tamilakam was ruled by:

  • Cheras
  • Cholas
  • Pandyas
  • Velir and other minor chieftains

The Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas were collectively known as the Muvendar or three crowned kings.

Major Sources
Tamil Sources
  • Tolkappiyam
  • Ettuthokai
  • Pattuppattu
  • Pathitrupattu
  • Purananuru
  • Akananuru
  • Pattinappalai
  • Maduraikanchi

The works and their literary features are covered in Chapter 4.

  • Ashoka’s Major Rock Edicts II and XIII
  • Mangulam Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions
  • Jambai inscription

  • Megasthenes

  • Keezhadi

Ashoka’s Edicts

Ashoka’s Major Rock Edicts II and XIII mention the southern powers:

  • Cholas
  • Pandyas
  • Satyaputras
  • Keralaputras
  • Tamraparni

These kingdoms lay outside Ashoka’s direct imperial territory.

Major Rock Edict II refers to medical arrangements for humans and animals in these neighbouring regions.

Major Rock Edict XIII refers to the spread of Dhamma among the southern kingdoms.

Hathigumpha Inscription
  • The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela, ruler of Kalinga, refers to a confederacy of Tamil countries.
  • The reading of the relevant expression and the duration assigned to the confederacy remain debated among epigraphists.
  • For examination purposes, remember:
  • Ruler — Kharavela
  • Dynasty — Mahameghavahana
  • Location — Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar
  • Reference — confederacy of Tamil rulers or countries
Political Map of Tamilakam

Tamilakam was not a single unified empire.

It contained:

  • Chera territory in the west
  • Chola territory in the Cauvery valley
  • Pandya territory in the south
  • Kongu region
  • Tondai region
  • Territories of Velir chiefs
  • Hill, pastoral and coastal chiefdoms

Royal authority depended on control over:

  • Fertile land
  • Rivers and irrigation
  • Ports
  • Trade routes
  • Warriors
  • Subordinate chiefs
The Chera Kingdom and Its Rulers

The Cheras controlled western Tamilakam and important inland and maritime routes. Literary titles, the Pugalur genealogy and Karur archaeology together illuminate their rulers and political world.

Chera Kingdom

Region: Western Tamilakam and parts of Kongu

Capital: Vanchi

Important inland centre: Karur

Major ports: Muchiri and Tondi

Emblem: Bow and arrow

Garland: Palmyra flower

Karur is frequently identified with an important Chera centre. The precise identification of every literary reference to Vanchi remains debated.

Pathitrupattu is the principal literary source for the early Chera rulers.

Uthiyan Cheralathan

Uthiyan Cheralathan is also known as Perunchotru Uthiyan Cheralathan.

Sangam tradition praises him for providing a great feast.

The literary claim that he fed the armies involved in the Mahabharata war is treated as poetic tradition rather than literal contemporary evidence.

Important association:

  • Uthiyan Cheralathan — Perunchotru or great feeding tradition
Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan

Neduncheralathan bore the title Imayavaramban.

The title means one whose boundary reached the Himalayas.

Sangam poems associate him with:

  • Northern military expedition
  • Maritime power
  • Conflict with Yavanas
  • Royal generosity

The Himalayan boundary should be understood as a literary claim of conquest or prestige, not proof of permanent Chera administration over northern India.

Cheran Senguttuvan

Cheran Senguttuvan was one of the most celebrated Chera rulers.

He was known as Kadal Pirakottiya Senguttuvan.

Pathitrupattu associates this title with action against pirates who interfered with merchant shipping.

He also fought Mokur Pazhayan according to the poems on his reign.

Silappadikaram later connects Senguttuvan with:

  • A northern expedition
  • Bringing a stone from the Himalayas
  • Consecration of Kannagi as Pattini

The Pattini account comes primarily from the later epic tradition.

Chera Irumporai Line

Several Chera rulers carried the title Irumporai.

Important rulers include:

  • Selvak Kadungo Vazhiyathan
  • Peruncheral Irumporai
  • Ilancheral Irumporai
  • Kanaikkal Irumporai

Peruncheral Irumporai is associated with the capture of Tagadur, the stronghold of the Adiyamans.

He received the title Tagadur Erindha Peruncheral Irumporai.

Kanaikkal Irumporai is remembered in literary tradition as a Chera ruler captured by the Chola king Sengannan.

Pugalur Inscriptions

The Pugalur or Aranattar Malai Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions near Karur mention three generations of a Chera family:

  • Ko Athan Chellirumporai
  • Perunkadungo
  • Ilankadungo

The inscriptions also record a donation to a Jain ascetic.

They provide important inscriptional evidence for:

  • Chera genealogy
  • Karur’s association with the Cheras
  • Jain patronage

Karur excavations have yielded Roman coins, precious stones, rouletted ware, amphora fragments and black-and-red ware.

The Chola Kingdom and Karikala

The Chola country centred on the Cauvery valley, Uraiyur and Puhar. Karikala’s victories, irrigation traditions and the Kallanai association form the core of early Chola political memory.

Chola Kingdom

Region: Cauvery valley and adjoining eastern plains

Capital: Uraiyur

Port and secondary capital: Kaveripoompattinam or Puhar

Emblem: Tiger

Garland: Athi flower

Major river: Cauvery

The Chola country was an important paddy-producing region.

Uraiyur was known for fine textiles, while Puhar developed as a major port and commercial centre.

Ilamchetchenni

Ilamchetchenni was an early Chola ruler and is traditionally identified as the father of Karikala Chola.

He is praised in Sangam poems for military ability.

The name Ilamchetchenni was used by more than one Chola ruler, making exact identification difficult.

Karikala Chola

Karikala was the most celebrated Chola ruler of the Sangam Age.

Battle of Venni

Karikala defeated a confederacy that included:

  • Chera ruler
  • Pandya ruler
  • Velir chieftains

The victory established his supremacy in the Chola region.

Vahaipparandalai

Karikala is also associated with a victory at Vahaipparandalai.

Agricultural Expansion

Literary tradition credits him with:

  • Clearing forest land
  • Expanding cultivation
  • Strengthening irrigation
  • Developing the Cauvery delta
  • Promoting Puhar
Kallanai

Karikala Chola is traditionally credited with constructing Kallanai, also known as the Grand Anicut, across the Cauvery.

Kallanai is a stone diversion structure designed to regulate and distribute river water into irrigation channels.

It is not a modern reservoir dam.

The structure became central to irrigation in the Cauvery delta and continues to function after later repairs and modifications. Government records continue to associate Kallanai with Karikala Chola.

Nalankilli and Nedunkilli

Nalankilli and Nedunkilli were rival Chola princes.

Their conflict resulted in:

  • Civil war
  • Siege of towns
  • Suffering among the population
  • Intervention and advice by poets

The rivalry shows that succession disputes weakened Chola authority during parts of the Sangam Age.

Perunarkilli

Perunarkilli is remembered by the title:

Rajasuyam Vetta Perunarkilli

The title indicates that he performed the Rajasuya sacrifice.

His performance of the ritual reflects the influence of Vedic concepts of kingship in Tamilakam.

Kochengannan
  • Kochengannan appears in early Tamil tradition as a Chola ruler.
  • Later Saiva tradition included him among the 63 Nayanmars and associated him with the construction of elevated temples known as Madakovils.
  • The religious accounts belong mainly to later Bhakti tradition and should not be used without caution for reconstructing the Sangam period.
The Pandya Kingdom and Its Rulers

The Pandyas ruled southern Tamilakam from Madurai and Korkai. Royal titles, Vedic ritual, the Talaiyalanganam victory and Mangulam inscriptions provide complementary evidence.

Pandya Kingdom

Region: Southern Tamilakam

Capital: Madurai

Early port: Korkai

Other port: Tondi

Emblem: Fish

Garland: Neem flower

Major rivers: Vaigai and Thamirabarani

Madurai was a political and cultural centre.

Korkai was associated with:

  • Pearl fishing
  • Conch collection
  • Maritime trade

The fish was the principal Pandya emblem.

Mudukudumi Peruvazhuthi

Mudukudumi Peruvazhuthi was known as:

Palyagasalai Mudukudumi Peruvazhuthi

The title Palyagasalai means the possessor of many sacrificial halls.

He is associated with:

  • Performance of Vedic sacrifices
  • Patronage of poets
  • Military expeditions
  • Gifts to learned persons

His title provides evidence for Vedic royal rituals among Sangam-age rulers.

Nedunchezhiyan of Talaiyalanganam

Nedunchezhiyan defeated a confederacy at the Battle of Talaiyalanganam.

The opposing alliance included:

  • Chera ruler
  • Chola ruler
  • Five Velir chiefs

He received the title:

Talaiyalanganathu Seruvendra Nedunchezhiyan

Maduraikanchi was composed in praise of a Pandya Nedunchezhiyan and describes Madurai and its administration.

More than one Pandya ruler carried the name Nedunchezhiyan.

Aryappadai Kadantha Nedunchezhiyan
  • A Pandya ruler bore the title:
  • Aryappadai Kadantha Nedunchezhiyan
  • The title means the ruler who overcame an Aryan or northern army.
  • Silappadikaram later identifies a ruler with this title as the Pandya king who ordered Kovalan’s execution.
  • The Kovalan episode belongs to epic tradition and is covered under post-Sangam literature.
Ukkirap Peruvazhuthi

Ukkirap Peruvazhuthi was an important Pandya ruler and poet.

Later literary tradition associates his court with the compilation of Akananuru.

The compilation and literary details belong to Chapter 4.

Mangulam Inscriptions

Mangulam near Madurai contains early Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions associated with:

  • Pandya ruler Nedunchezhiyan
  • Royal workers or officials
  • Jain ascetics
  • Merchant patronage

The inscriptions record the provision of stone beds or hermitages for Jain monks.

Mangulam provides direct evidence connecting an early Pandya ruler with Tamil-Brahmi writing and Jain patronage.

Velir Chiefs and the Great Patrons

Velir and Kurunila Mannar controlled smaller territories and strategic routes. The seven great patrons became enduring symbols of generosity, resistance and poet–patron relationships.

Velir and Kurunila Mannar

Alongside the Muvendar, several minor chieftains ruled hill regions, forest routes, river valleys and smaller agricultural territories.

They were known as:

  • Velir
  • Kurunila Mannar
  • Kizhar

Some supported the Muvendar, while others resisted their expansion.

Kadaiyezhu Vallalgal

The last seven celebrated patrons were:

  • Pari
  • Kari
  • Ori
  • Pegan
  • Ay
  • Adiyaman
  • Nalli

They were remembered for extraordinary generosity.

The list appears in Tamil literary tradition and became a major symbol of ideal patronage.

Vel Pari

Territory: Parambu Nadu

Associated poet: Kapilar

Pari resisted the combined pressure of the three crowned kings.

He is remembered for giving his chariot to support a jasmine creeper.

After Pari’s death, Kapilar took responsibility for his daughters:

  • Angavai
  • Sangavai

Pari represents the resistance of independent hill chiefs to the expanding Muvendar.

Adiyaman Neduman Anji

Capital: Tagadur

Modern association: Dharmapuri region

Associated poet: Avvaiyar

Literary tradition states that Adiyaman gave a rare gooseberry believed to prolong life to Avvaiyar.

The Jambai Tamil-Brahmi inscription reads:

Satiyaputo Atiyan Netuman Anci itta Pali

It identifies Adiyaman Neduman Anji as Satyaputra, linking him with the Satyaputras mentioned in Ashoka’s edicts.

Valvil Ori

Territory: Kolli Hills

Ori was celebrated for:

  • Archery
  • Bravery
  • Generosity

He was known as Valvil Ori, meaning Ori of the powerful bow.

Malaiyaman Tirumudikkari

Centre: Tirukkovilur

River region: South Pennaiyar

Kari controlled an important route between the eastern plains and the interior.

He was involved in conflicts among the Cheras, Cholas and minor chiefs.

Pegan

Pegan ruled a cold hill region.

Literary tradition states that he gave his cloak to a peacock suffering from the cold.

The story symbolised unlimited generosity.

Ay Andiran

Ay Andiran ruled the southern hill region near the Podhigai mountains.

The Ay chiefs controlled routes between the Tamil plains and the western coast.

Nalli

Nalli was remembered for:

  • Hospitality
  • Protection of visitors
  • Generous gifts

His territory is associated with the hill regions of northern or western Tamilakam in literary traditions.

Kingship and Administrative Councils

Sangam kingship was hereditary but supported by organised groups of ministers, priests, military commanders, envoys, spies, accountants and specialised officers.

Kingship

Kingship was generally hereditary.

Important royal titles included:

  • Ko
  • Kon
  • Vendan
  • Mannan
  • Kotravan
  • Iraivan

The crown prince was called Komagan or Ilango in different contexts.

Important royal symbols included:

  • Crown
  • Sceptre
  • White umbrella
  • Royal drum
  • Flag
  • Garland

The Senkol, or straight sceptre, symbolised just rule.

Aimperumkuzhu

The Aimperumkuzhu was the council of five major officials.

It is commonly listed as including:

  • Amaichar — minister
  • Purohitar — priest
  • Thanaithalaivar — military commander
  • Thoothuvar — envoy
  • Saranar — spy or intelligence officer
Enperayam

The Enperayam was the council of eight groups of officers.

The members are commonly identified as:

  • Karanathiyalavar — accountants
  • Karumakarar — executive officials
  • Kanakasutram — treasury officials
  • Kadaikappalar — guards
  • Nagaramanthar — representatives of towns
  • Padaithalaivar — military officers
  • Yanaiveerar — elephant corps officers
  • Ivuli Maravar — cavalry officers

The Tamil Virtual Academy identifies Aimperumkuzhu and Enperayam as important administrative bodies of the Sangam Age.

Administrative Units, Court, Revenue and Justice

Territorial terms, the Arasavai, taxation and justice show how rulers organised settlements, collected resources and were expected to uphold the Senkol or just rule.

Administrative Units

Important territorial and settlement terms included:

  • Nadu — territory or region
  • Kurram — smaller territorial division
  • Ur — village or settlement
  • Sirur — small settlement
  • Perur — large settlement
  • Pattinam — commercial or port town

The divisions were not as standardised as the administrative units of the later imperial Cholas.

Royal Court

The royal court was known as the Arasavai.

The king was assisted by:

  • Ministers
  • Commanders
  • Envoys
  • Spies
  • Priests
  • Accountants
  • Poets

The king’s daily public assembly was called Naalavai.

Poets could advise rulers, carry diplomatic messages and intervene during political conflicts.

Revenue

Important sources of state revenue included:

  • Irai — tax or tribute, especially land revenue
  • Sungam or Ulgu — customs duty
  • Thirai — tribute paid by subordinate rulers
  • Market tolls
  • Fines
  • War booty
  • Gifts from subordinate chiefs

Customs collected at ports and roads formed an important source of income.

Justice

The king was the highest judicial authority.

The ruler was expected to:

  • Hear petitions
  • Protect subjects
  • Punish criminals
  • Prevent excessive taxation
  • Maintain the Senkol or just rule

The Avai and Mandram were associated with deliberation and local public activity.

Punishments included fines, imprisonment, bodily punishment and execution.

Military Organisation and Heroic Memory

The fourfold army, cattle raids and hero stones reveal the material and cultural organisation of warfare, honour, protection and public remembrance.

Fourfold Army

The army consisted of:

  • Infantry
  • Cavalry
  • Elephant corps
  • Chariot force

The commander was called Thanaithalaivan.

Important weapons included:

  • Sword
  • Spear
  • Bow and arrow
  • Shield
  • Javelin

Forts were protected by walls, gates and moats.

Cattle Raids and Warfare

Cattle were an important form of wealth.

Raiding enemy cattle could provoke warfare.

Puram poetic convention classified stages of war through terms such as:

  • Vetchi — cattle raid
  • Vanchi — invasion
  • Uzhinjai — siege
  • Thumbai — battle
  • Vaagai — victory

The complete literary classification belongs to Chapter 4.

Hero Stones

A Nadukal or hero stone was erected for a person who died while protecting:

  • Cattle
  • Village
  • Territory
  • Community

The warrior’s figure and deed could be carved on the stone.

Hero stones later became objects of remembrance and worship.

Agriculture, Irrigation and Industries

Agriculture depended on fertile river valleys, cattle and irrigation. Weaving, metallurgy, bead making, salt, shell work and shipbuilding created specialised production centres.

Agriculture

Major crops included:

  • Paddy
  • Millets
  • Sugarcane
  • Pulses
  • Cotton
  • Sesame

The important agricultural regions were:

  • Cauvery delta
  • Vaigai valley
  • Thamirabarani valley

Agricultural tools included ploughs, sickles and iron implements.

Cattle were used for ploughing and transport.

Irrigation

Sources of irrigation included:

  • Rivers
  • Tanks
  • Wells
  • Channels
  • Bunds
  • Diversion structures

Kallanai helped divert Cauvery water into deltaic channels.

Rulers who protected irrigation and expanded cultivation were praised in Sangam literature.

Industries

Important industries included:

  • Cotton weaving
  • Pottery
  • Iron working
  • Steel production
  • Bead making
  • Goldsmithing
  • Shell working
  • Salt production
  • Shipbuilding

Kodumanal was an important centre of bead production and iron working.

Uraiyur was associated with fine cotton textiles.

Korkai was associated with pearls and conch products.

Internal Trade and Markets

Internal exchange moved food, salt, dairy products, forest goods and manufactured items between ecological regions. Day and night markets concentrated trade in major towns.

Internal Trade

Products moved between the five ecological regions.

Examples include:

  • Paddy from agricultural plains
  • Salt and fish from the coast
  • Milk products from pastoral regions
  • Honey and forest products from hill regions
  • Beads, textiles and iron products from craft centres

Goods were transported by:

  • Bullock carts
  • Pack animals
  • Merchant caravans
  • River boats
  • Coastal vessels

Barter and coin-based exchange existed together.

Markets
Nalangadi

Daytime market.

Allangadi

Evening or night market.

Market centres sold:

  • Grain
  • Fish
  • Meat
  • Salt
  • Textiles
  • Flowers
  • Jewellery
  • Liquor
  • Imported goods

Puhar and Madurai contained specialised market streets and warehouses.

Yavanas, Ports, Exports and Imports

Yavana traders, major ports, exports and imports placed Tamilakam within the Indian Ocean commercial system. Dynasty–port associations remain especially important for revision.

Yavanas
  • The term Yavana was used for western foreigners.
  • Depending on the period and context, it could refer to:
  • Greeks
  • Romans
  • Traders from the western world
  • Sangam poems refer to Yavana ships, wine, lamps and guards.
  • The term should not always be translated narrowly as “Roman”.
Major Ports
Muchiri
  • Chera port
  • Associated with pepper trade
  • Known as Muziris in Greco-Roman sources
Tondi
  • Port associated mainly with the Chera region
  • More than one ancient port may have carried this name
Puhar
  • Chola port
  • Also called Kaveripoompattinam
  • Located near the mouth of the Cauvery
Korkai
  • Pandya port
  • Associated with pearls and conch fishing

The ports of Muchiri, Puhar and Korkai are important dynasty-port associations. The Periplus also refers to ports along the Tamil coast.

Exports

Important exports included:

  • Pepper
  • Pearls
  • Ivory
  • Gemstones
  • Beryl
  • Cotton textiles
  • Spices
  • Aromatic woods
  • Tortoise shell
  • Iron and steel products

Pepper was strongly associated with the western coast.

Pearls were strongly associated with the Pandya coast.

Imports

Important imports included:

  • Gold and silver coins
  • Wine
  • Coral
  • Glassware
  • Luxury pottery
  • Tin and metals
  • Horses

Amphora fragments found at Tamil sites are associated with imported wine, oil or other liquids.

Foreign Accounts and Coin Evidence

The Periplus, Pliny, Ptolemy and coin finds provide external and material evidence for ports, routes, commodities and the movement of precious metals.

Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea was written by an anonymous Greek-speaking merchant in the first century CE.

It provides information about:

  • Ports
  • Sailing routes
  • Commodities
  • Merchant activity
  • Coastal kingdoms

It mentions or helps identify ports such as:

  • Muziris
  • Tyndis
  • Korkai region
  • Poduke or Arikamedu
Pliny the Elder

Pliny wrote Natural History in the first century CE.

He complained about the flow of Roman gold towards India in payment for luxury goods.

His account reflects the favourable balance enjoyed by Indian merchants in Indo-Roman trade.

Ptolemy

Ptolemy wrote Geography during the second century CE.

His work refers to southern Indian:

  • Ports
  • Rivers
  • Inland towns
  • Coastal routes

Names recorded in Greek form must be matched cautiously with modern locations.

Coins

Coins used during the period included:

  • Punch-marked coins
  • Local copper and lead coins
  • Chera coins
  • Chola coins
  • Pandya coins
  • Roman gold, silver and copper coins

Dynastic symbols included:

  • Bow and arrow — Cheras
  • Tiger — Cholas
  • Fish — Pandyas

Foreign coins could be used as:

  • Currency
  • Bullion
  • Jewellery
  • Stored wealth

Roman coin finds are concentrated in commercial and inland-route regions such as Karur and the Kongu area.

Religious Life in the Sangam Age

Sangam religion combined landscape deities, Vedic rituals and Jain and Buddhist monastic activity. These traditions coexisted rather than replacing one another in a single stage.

Major Deities

Important deities included:

  • Seyon or Murugan
  • Mayon or Thirumal
  • Korravai
  • Vendan or Indra
  • Varunan
  • Sivan
  • Balarama or Valiyon in selected traditions

Murugan was strongly associated with hill worship.

Korravai was connected with warfare and victory.

Vedic Practices

Sangam sources refer to:

  • Anthanar
  • Vedic learning
  • Fire sacrifices
  • Rajasuya
  • Yagas

Important ruler-ritual associations:

  • Mudukudumi Peruvazhuthi — Palyagasalai
  • Perunarkilli — Rajasuya sacrifice

Vedic practices existed alongside older Tamil religious traditions.

Jainism and Buddhism

Tamil-Brahmi cave inscriptions record donations to Jain ascetics.

Important Jain-associated sites include:

  • Mangulam
  • Pugalur
  • Arittapatti
  • Alagarmalai
  • Jambai

Buddhist connections were stronger at coastal and urban centres and became more prominent in later literature.

Political Transition and the Sangam-Maruvia Phase

From around the third century CE, the early Muvendar order gradually changed. The transition led into Kalabhra influence and the wider Sangam-Maruvia or post-Sangam phase.

Political Transition

From approximately the third century CE, the political order associated with the classical Sangam Age weakened.

The transition involved:

  • Decline of early Muvendar power
  • Changes in maritime commerce
  • Political conflicts
  • Growth of new ruling groups
  • Expansion of Jain and Buddhist influence

The Kalabhras subsequently gained control over major parts of Tamilakam.

The transition from the Sangam to the post-Sangam phase is known as the Sangam-Maruvia period.

Rapid Revision and Important Distinctions

Rapid Revision and Important Distinctions consolidate dynasty–capital–emblem–port links, rulers, inscriptions, administration, trade and common examination traps.

Rapid Revision
Muvendar
  • Chera — Vanchi/Karur — bow and arrow — Muchiri
  • Chola — Uraiyur — tiger — Puhar
  • Pandya — Madurai — fish — Korkai
Chera Rulers
  • Uthiyan Cheralathan — Perunchotru tradition
  • Neduncheralathan — Imayavaramban
  • Senguttuvan — Kadal Pirakottiya
  • Peruncheral Irumporai — Tagadur Erindha
  • Pugalur inscription — Chera genealogy
Chola Rulers
  • Ilamchetchenni — father of Karikala in tradition
  • Karikala — Venni, Vahaipparandalai and Kallanai
  • Nalankilli and Nedunkilli — rival Chola princes
  • Perunarkilli — Rajasuya sacrifice
Pandya Rulers
  • Mudukudumi Peruvazhuthi — Palyagasalai
  • Nedunchezhiyan — victory at Talaiyalanganam
  • Aryappadai Kadantha Nedunchezhiyan — northern army title
  • Ukkirap Peruvazhuthi — associated with Akananuru compilation
Minor Chiefs
  • Pari — Parambu — Kapilar
  • Adiyaman Neduman Anji — Tagadur — Avvaiyar
  • Ori — Kolli Hills
  • Kari — Tirukkovilur
  • Ay Andiran — Podhigai region
  • Pegan — hill chief
  • Nalli — generosity
Inscriptions
  • Ashoka — Cholas, Pandyas, Satyaputras and Keralaputras
  • Mangulam — Pandya Nedunchezhiyan and Jain beds
  • Jambai — Adiyaman Neduman Anji as Satyaputra
  • Pugalur — Chera genealogy
  • Hathigumpha — Tamil confederacy reference
Administration
  • Aimperumkuzhu — council of five
  • Enperayam — council of eight groups
  • Irai — tax or tribute
  • Sungam or Ulgu — customs duty
  • Thirai — tribute from subordinate ruler
  • Arasavai — royal court
  • Naalavai — daily assembly
Economy
  • Kallanai — Karikala Chola
  • Nalangadi — day market
  • Allangadi — night market
  • Kodumanal — beads and iron
  • Uraiyur — cotton textiles
  • Korkai — pearls and conch
  • Muchiri — pepper
  • Puhar — Chola maritime trade
Foreign Sources
  • Ashoka — Major Rock Edicts II and XIII
  • Periplus — ports and maritime trade
  • Pliny — drain of Roman gold
  • Ptolemy — geographical information
  • Kharavela — Hathigumpha inscription
Important Distinctions
  • Karikala Chola belongs to the Sangam Age; Aditya Karikala belongs to the medieval imperial Chola period.
  • Kallanai is primarily a water-diversion structure, not a modern storage dam.
  • Senguttuvan’s Pattini consecration is recorded mainly in the later Silappadikaram tradition.
  • Jambai inscription identifies Adiyaman as Satyaputra; Ashoka’s edicts mention the Satyaputras without naming Adiyaman.
  • Vanchi’s exact location remains debated, though Karur was an important Chera centre.
  • More than one Chera, Chola and Pandya ruler used similar names and titles.
  • Yavana does not always mean only Roman.
  • Roman coins prove commercial contact, but not Roman political rule over Tamilakam.
